page: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard.E3.Flex.32-128 is a virtual machine configuration within the flexible E3 compute family, delivering dedicated x86_64 computing resources. The instance is powered by an AMD EPYC 7742 processor operating at a base clock frequency of 2.25 GHz. It is provisioned with 32 physical cores and 64 virtual central processing units (vCPUs) via simultaneous multithreading, alongside 128.0 GB of system memory. This resource profile yields a 1:2 vCPU-to-memory allocation of 2.0 GB RAM per vCPU.

Hardware acceleration is not included, as the instance features zero GPUs. In addition, no local NVMe storage is bundled, requiring workloads to rely exclusively on remote block volumes or network-attached file storage for non-volatile data persistence. Network connectivity includes one complimentary public IPv4 address for external ingress and egress traffic.

The 1:2 memory-to-vCPU ratio establishes high core density relative to memory capacity, prioritizing parallel compute throughput over massive per-thread memory footprint. This configuration is suitable for distributed compilation tasks, batch compute pipelines, container host orchestration, continuous integration and deployment runners, and compute-bound web serving fleets.
description: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard.E3.Flex.32-128 is a flexible compute instance powered by an AMD EPYC 7742 x86_64 processor clocked at 2.25 GHz. The virtual machine provides 32 dedicated physical cores, 64 vCPUs, and 128.0 GB of system memory, maintaining a 1:2 vCPU-to-memory ratio. It contains no dedicated GPU hardware and does not include bundled local NVMe storage, meaning operational data persistence depends entirely on remote block or network storage solutions. One complimentary public IPv4 address is included. With a dense 64-vCPU footprint, the instance emphasizes thread-parallel execution over per-thread memory allocation. This profile is engineered for compute-centric multi-threaded workloads, including CI/CD automation pipelines, batch processing jobs, video encoding queues, and microservices hosting.
